title: Understanding whoami
description: whoami displays information about the currently logged-on user and their security context (account name, SID, groups, and privileges) on Windows.
summary: whoami displays information about the currently logged-on user and their security context (account name, SID, groups, and privileges) on Windows.

examples.description: Shows the current user in DOMAIN\User or COMPUTERNAME\User format.
Displays the current user as a User Principal Name (UPN), e.g., user@contoso.com (requires domain account).
Displays the user name using the domain's fully qualified domain name (FQDN), e.g., corp.contoso.com\user (requires domain context).
Shows the current user and their Security Identifier (SID).
Lists group memberships and attributes (e.g., Mandatory, Enabled, Deny-only).
Lists security privileges in the current logon token and whether each is enabled or disabled.
Displays comprehensive identity details: user, SID, groups, privileges, and logon information.
Shows the hexadecimal logon session ID (LUID) for the current session.

important_fields.description: Reveals the user and SID; useful to confirm which account (and SID) the process is running under.
Indicates group influence on access (e.g., Deny-only, Mandatory, Enabled by default). Critical when troubleshooting permission issues.
Shows whether sensitive privileges (e.g., SeBackupPrivilege) are enabled; affects ability to perform certain actions.
Identifies the specific logon session (LUID), helping correlate with security logs or session diagnostics.
Outputs user@domain format; helpful for SSO/Kerberos troubleshooting in domain environments.
Displays the user with the domain’s FQDN; helps avoid ambiguity with NetBIOS names.

common_errors.error: 'whoami' is not recognized as an internal or external command, operable program or batch file.
common_errors.description: Occurs if system paths to System32 are missing from PATH, the binary is unavailable, or on very old/stripped environments. Run from %SystemRoot%\System32 or fix PATH.

common_errors.error: ERROR: Invalid syntax. Type "WHOAMI /?" for usage.
common_errors.description: Triggered by unsupported or misspelled switches (e.g., /domain). Use whoami /? to see valid options.

common_errors.error: UPN/FQDN not available for this account.
common_errors.description: The account is local or the system cannot contact a domain controller. Ensure the user is a domain account and the DC is reachable.

common_errors.error: Insufficient resources to complete the operation.
common_errors.description: Rare; indicates a transient system resource issue when querying token details. Retry or check system health.

explanation.title: Understanding the command
explanation.purpose: whoami verifies the exact security context of the current process, including account, groups, and privileges. This is essential for diagnosing access denials, elevation issues, and domain identity problems.
explanation.when_to_use: Use whoami when permissions fail unexpectedly, scripts run under the wrong account, domain name ambiguity exists, or when validating that required privileges/groups are present before attempting protected actions.

what_to_check.name: Account name and domain (base output, /upn, /fqdn)
what_to_check.description: Confirms you’re operating under the expected identity and domain namespace.

what_to_check.name: SID (/user)
what_to_check.description: Verifies the unique security identifier mapped to the account; helpful when ACLs reference SIDs.

what_to_check.name: Group Attributes (/groups)
what_to_check.description: Shows whether a group is Deny-only, Mandatory, or Enabled; explains why access is allowed/denied.

what_to_check.name: Privilege State (/priv)
what_to_check.description: Determines if needed privileges (e.g., SeTcbPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege) are available and enabled.

what_to_check.name: Logon ID (/logonid)
what_to_check.description: Correlates the running session with Security event logs and session-based diagnostics.

interpretation.title: Output shows NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or a service account
interpretation.message: The process is running under a high-privilege or service context. Verify least-privilege, and confirm group/privilege sets before making system changes.

interpretation.title: Expected group missing or marked Deny-only
interpretation.message: Access may fail even if you belong to the group. Investigate token filtering, UAC split tokens, or nested group resolution.

interpretation.title: Required privilege listed as Disabled
interpretation.message: Operation requiring that privilege will fail. Enable it in the process token (where applicable) or run under an account with the privilege.

interpretation.title: UPN/FQDN not returned
interpretation.message: Likely a local account or no domain controller connectivity. Check network and domain membership.

explanation.common_mistake: Assuming successful logon equals correct privileges—technicians often check only whoami without reviewing /groups or /priv, missing disabled privileges or Deny-only groups.
explanation.permissions_notes: whoami reads the current token and does not modify system state. It works for standard users; some fields may vary based on token filtering or service contexts.
explanation.risk_warning: Reveals identity and security details to the console; avoid sharing outputs that contain sensitive SIDs or account names.

next_steps.name: gpresult
next_steps.summary: Correlate whoami results with applied Group Policy to understand why groups/privileges are present or missing.

next_steps.name: net
next_steps.summary: Inspect account properties and local group memberships to validate what whoami reported.

next_steps.name: query
next_steps.summary: Map the logon session to active user sessions when multiple users or services are running.

next_steps.name: klist
next_steps.summary: If using domain credentials, check Kerberos tickets to validate domain identity and troubleshooting SSO issues surfaced by whoami.

explanation.narrative: First I run whoami to confirm the exact identity and domain namespace. If the base output isn’t what I expect, I check whoami /upn and /fqdn for domain clarity. Then I run whoami /groups and /priv to see whether the necessary groups and privileges are present and enabled. If something’s off, I follow up with gpresult to see policies affecting the token, query user to confirm the active session, and klist to verify Kerberos state in a domain scenario.
